**Claim:** Yes. There exist $c_1,\dots,c_n\in k$ with $f(c_1,\dots,c_n)\neq 0$.

**Proof.**

Since $K/k$ is a finite extension, $K$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space. Choose a $k$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_m$ of $K$ (with $e_1=1$ WLOG, though this is not essential). Every coefficient of $f$ lies in $K$, hence expands uniquely as a $k$-linear combination of $e_1,\dots,e_m$. By $k$-linearity of polynomial evaluation, for any $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ we may write

$$
f(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\sum_{i=1}^{m} e_i\, f_i(x_1,\dots,x_n),
$$

where each $f_i\in k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is a polynomial over $k$. (Expand every coefficient of $f$ in the basis and collect terms multiplying each $e_i$.)

Because $e_1,\dots,e_m$ are $k$-linearly independent, for any point $(c_1,\dots,c_n)\in k^n$,

$$
f(c_1,\dots,c_n)=0 \iff f_i(c_1,\dots,c_n)=0\ \text{for all } i=1,\dots,m. \tag{$\ast$}
$$

Since $f$ is non-constant, $f\neq 0$, so at least one $f_i$ is a **nonzero** polynomial. Let

$$
S=\{\,i\in\{1,\dots,m\}: f_i\neq 0 \text{ in } k[x_1,\dots,x_n]\,\}.
$$

$S\neq\varnothing$. Consider the product

$$
g(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{i\in S} f_i(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in k[x_1,\dots,x_n].
$$

Since $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is an integral domain and each factor is nonzero, $g$ is a **nonzero** polynomial.

**Key fact.** *A nonzero polynomial over an infinite field does not vanish identically on $k^n$.* This is proved by induction on $n$: for $n=1$ a nonzero univariate polynomial of degree $d$ has at most $d$ roots, so it cannot vanish on the infinite set $k$. For $n>1$, write $g=\sum_{j=0}^{D} g_j(x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})\,x_n^{\,j}$ with $g_D\neq 0$; by induction there exists $(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})\in k^{n-1}$ with $g_D(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})\neq 0$, and then $g(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1},x_n)$ is a nonzero univariate polynomial in $x_n$, which has only finitely many roots over the infinite field $k$; picking $a_n\in k$ outside that finite set gives $g(a_1,\dots,a_n)\neq 0$.

Applying this to the nonzero polynomial $g$ over the infinite field $k$, there exists $(c_1,\dots,c_n)\in k^n$ with

$$
g(c_1,\dots,c_n)=\prod_{i\in S}f_i(c_1,\dots,c_n)\neq 0.
$$

Hence $f_i(c_1,\dots,c_n)\neq 0$ for every $i\in S$ (in particular for at least one $i$). By the equivalence ($\ast$), since some $f_i(c_1,\dots,c_n)\neq 0$,

$$
f(c_1,\dots,c_n)=\sum_{i=1}^{m} e_i\, f_i(c_1,\dots,c_n)\neq 0.
$$

Thus $c_1,\dots,c_n\in k$ with $f(c_1,\dots,c_n)\neq 0$ exist. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
